<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">A Single Image and Multimodality Is All You Need for Novel View Synthesis</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Amirhosein Javadi
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chi-Shiang Gau
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Konstantinos D. Polyzos
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tara Javidi
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of California San Diego
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{amjavadi,cgau,kpolyzos,tjavidi}@ucsd.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion-based approaches have recently demonstrated strong performance for single-image novel view synthesis by conditioning generative models on geometry inferred from monocular depth estimation. However, in practice, the quality and consistency of the synthesized views are fundamentally limited by the reliability of the underlying depth estimates, which are often fragile under low texture, adverse weather, and occlusion-heavy real-world conditions. In this work, we show that incorporating sparse multimodal range measurements provides a simple yet effective way to overcome these limitations. We introduce a multimodal depth reconstruction framework that leverages extremely sparse range sensing data, such as automotive radar or LiDAR, to produce dense depth maps that serve as robust geometric conditioning for diffusion-based novel view synthesis. Our approach models depth in an angular domain using a localized Gaussian Process formulation, enabling computationally efficient inference while explicitly quantifying uncertainty in regions with limited observations. The reconstructed depth and uncertainty are used as a drop-in replacement for monocular depth estimators in existing diffusion-based rendering pipelines, without modifying the generative model itself. Experiments on real-world multimodal driving scenes demonstrate that replacing vision-only depth with our sparse range–based reconstruction substantially improves both geometric consistency and visual quality in single-image novel-view video generation. These results highlight the importance of reliable geometric priors for diffusion-based view synthesis and demonstrate the practical benefits of multimodal sensing even at extreme levels of sparsity.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Synthesizing accurate images from novel viewpoints, commonly referred to as novel-view synthesis, is a fundamental problem with broad applications in virtual reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. Accurate geometric representations are critical for producing visually consistent novel views, particularly when only limited visual observations are available. While novel-view synthesis and 3D scene rendering have been studied for decades, reconstruction-based approaches such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mildenhall et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barron et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and Gaussian Splatting (GS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kerbl et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polyzos et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> have recently demonstrated impressive rendering fidelity by explicitly modeling scene geometry from multi-view observations. However, these methods typically require dense image sets with high viewpoint coverage to achieve high-quality reconstructions, making them impractical in settings where only sparse or single-view observations are available.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address sparse-view scenarios, generative approaches have emerged as an alternative to reconstruction-based models, aiming to synthesize plausible novel views without explicitly recovering full 3D scene representations. In the particularly challenging single-image setting, recent diffusion-based rendering pipelines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite> typically operate by first estimating depth from the input image and constructing an intermediate 3D representation, such as a point cloud, which is rendered along a target camera trajectory. A diffusion model is then conditioned on these rendered views to hallucinate missing content in disoccluded or unobserved regions, producing visually coherent novel views. While this paradigm has shown strong empirical performance compared to reconstruction-based methods in single-view settings, its effectiveness critically depends on the accuracy and consistency of the underlying depth estimates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Monocular depth estimation from a single RGB image is inherently ill-posed, and existing approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> rely heavily on learned visual priors. In real-world environments, factors such as weak texture, challenging illumination, adverse weather, and occlusions frequently lead to depth predictions that are inaccurate or spatially inconsistent. In diffusion-based novel-view synthesis pipelines, these errors are not isolated: they are amplified through geometric back-projection and rendering, propagating across viewpoints and resulting in misalignment artifacts, inconsistent geometry, and degraded temporal coherence in the generated views. This observation highlights the need for improving the robustness of geometric initialization to enable reliable single-image novel-view synthesis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to existing vision-only approaches, in the present work we introduce a multimodal diffusion-based approach for efficient novel view synthesis, whose contributions can be contextualized in the following aspects:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a range-sensor–based depth reconstruction module that leverages sparse radar or LiDAR measurements and serves as a drop-in replacement for vision-only monocular depth estimators in diffusion-based novel-view synthesis pipelines, while remaining agnostic to the diffusion model itself.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using only sparse range measurements, we propose an efficient depth reconstruction approach based on localized Gaussian Process modeling. By partitioning the image into spatially localized regions and fitting independent local Gaussian Processes, our method achieves improved computational efficiency while producing dense depth estimates with well-calibrated uncertainty.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Experiments on real-world multimodal autonomous driving data demonstrate consistent improvements over image-only baselines. Replacing monocular depth with our multimodal reconstruction reduces LPIPS by 23.5% and FID by 46.0% in single-image novel-view video generation, while also improving depth accuracy, reducing mean absolute error by 4.5% when evaluated against LiDAR ground truth.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Geometry-Conditioned Diffusion for Novel-View Synthesis</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a fixed noising process.
Given a clean sample <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}\sim p_{\text{data}}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>data</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}\sim p_{\text{data}}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, the forward diffusion process produces</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\tau}=\alpha_{\tau}x_{0}+\sigma_{\tau}\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\tau}=\alpha_{\tau}x_{0}+\sigma_{\tau}\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the diffusion time and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\alpha_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\alpha_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau}\}</annotation></semantics></math> follow a
predefined noise schedule.
A denoising network <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is trained to predict the injected noise, conditioned on auxiliary
information <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, by minimizing</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\epsilon,\tau}\left[\left\|f_{\theta}(x_{\tau},\tau;c)-\epsilon\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\epsilon,\tau}\left[\left\|f_{\theta}(x_{\tau},\tau;c)-\epsilon\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">After training, novel samples are generated by iteratively applying the learned reverse process,
starting from Gaussian noise and guided by the conditioning signal. In this work, we use a standard
diffusion formulation and do not modify the generative model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In sparse-view novel-view synthesis, the conditioning signal <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is derived from an explicit
geometric initialization in the form of rendered novel-view frames.
Given an input image <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> and camera intrinsics
<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐊</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math>, a depth estimator <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> produces a depth map
<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z=D(I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z=D(I)</annotation></semantics></math> for pixel coordinates <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{p}}=[u,v,1]^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{p}}=[u,v,1]^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> denote homogeneous image coordinates.
The corresponding 3D point in the camera frame is obtained via standard back-projection:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}Z(u,v)\,\frac{u-c_{x}}{f_{x}}\\
Z(u,v)\,\frac{v-c_{y}}{f_{y}}\\
Z(u,v)\end{bmatrix}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>cam</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}Z(u,v)\,\frac{u-c_{x}}{f_{x}}\\
Z(u,v)\,\frac{v-c_{y}}{f_{y}}\\
Z(u,v)\end{bmatrix}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Associating each <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>cam</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> with its pixel color <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> yields a colored point
cloud</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of valid pixels.
Given a target camera pose <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{T}_{t}=[\mathbf{R}_{t}\mid\mathbf{t}_{t}]\in SE(3)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐓</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐭</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{T}_{t}=[\mathbf{R}_{t}\mid\mathbf{t}_{t}]\in SE(3)</annotation></semantics></math>, each 3D point
is transformed to the target camera frame:</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}^{(t)}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)=\mathbf{R}_{t}\,\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)+\mathbf{t}_{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>cam</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mtext>cam</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐭</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}^{(t)}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)=\mathbf{R}_{t}\,\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(u,v)+\mathbf{t}_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">The transformed points are projected to the target image plane using the pinhole camera model:</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}^{(t)}=\begin{bmatrix}u^{(t)}\\
v^{(t)}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}f_{x}\,x^{(t)}/z^{(t)}+c_{x}\\
f_{y}\,y^{(t)}/z^{(t)}+c_{y}\end{bmatrix}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><msup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}^{(t)}=\begin{bmatrix}u^{(t)}\\
v^{(t)}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}f_{x}\,x^{(t)}/z^{(t)}+c_{x}\\
f_{y}\,y^{(t)}/z^{(t)}+c_{y}\end{bmatrix}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.5" class="ltx_p">Finally, the conditioning frame <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained by splatting
each colored point <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{p}^{(t)},I(u,v))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{p}^{(t)},I(u,v))</annotation></semantics></math> onto the target image plane:</p>
<table id="S2.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}=\mathrm{Splat}\!\left(\left\{\big(\mathbf{p}^{(t)}(u,v),\,I(u,v)\big)\right\}_{(u,v)\in\Omega}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.212em;" width="2.212em"><mi>Splat</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}=\mathrm{Splat}\!\left(\left\{\big(\mathbf{p}^{(t)}(u,v),\,I(u,v)\big)\right\}_{(u,v)\in\Omega}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.6" class="ltx_p">For a target camera trajectory consisting of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> viewpoints, the diffusion model is conditioned on
the sequence of rendered frames <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=\{c_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=\{c_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These conditioning frames depend entirely on the estimated depth <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math>.
Errors in <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> induce geometric misalignment across viewpoints, which propagate through the diffusion
process and result in view-dependent artifacts and degraded temporal consistency in the synthesized
views.
In this work, we replace the image-only depth estimator <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> with a range-sensor–driven depth
reconstruction module, while keeping the unprojection, rendering, and diffusion components
unchanged.
The depth reconstruction is performed independently of the diffusion model and serves as a
drop-in geometric prior. An overview of the full geometry-conditioned diffusion pipeline is shown in Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Single View to Video Generation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ A Single Image and Multimodality Is All You Need for Novel View Synthesis" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17909v1/pipeline.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/247;" width="548" height="247" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
Overview of the proposed multimodal single-image novel-view synthesis pipeline. Sparse range sensing measurements are first processed by the proposed GP-based depth reconstruction module to produce a dense depth map. The reconstructed depth and the input RGB image are used to form a colored 3D point cloud, which is rendered along a target camera trajectory to generate sparse novel-view conditioning frames. These rendered frames are provided as geometric conditioning to a diffusion model, which synthesizes a temporally consistent video at the target viewpoints.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Sparse Range-Sensor Depth Estimation via Gaussian Processes</h3>

<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17909v1/localGP_illustration.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/278;" width="494" height="278" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Illustration of the proposed localized Gaussian Process depth reconstruction in the angular domain. Left: Sparse radar range measurements represented in azimuth–elevation space, with the current target viewing direction indicated. Right: Zoomed-in view around the target location, highlighting the local neighborhood used for Gaussian Process inference. Only range measurements within this localized region contribute to the depth estimation at the target direction, enabling efficient and spatially adaptive depth reconstruction from sparse observations.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a single acquisition from a sparse range sensing modality, such as radar or LiDAR,
which provides an unordered set of 3D range points without color information. These points are
mapped to azimuth and elevation angles, yielding a set of sparse depth measurements
<math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{T}=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{T}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{T}=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{T}]</annotation></semantics></math> at corresponding sensing directions.
Our objective is to reconstruct a dense depth map aligned with the image plane of a single RGB
input, while explicitly modeling uncertainty in regions with limited or no range observations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To establish a geometrically consistent representation, we operate in an angular domain shared by
both sparse range measurements and image pixels.
Each range measurement is represented by its azimuth and elevation angles
<math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{t}=(\phi_{t},\theta_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{t}=(\phi_{t},\theta_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and its measured depth <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For each image pixel <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute the corresponding camera ray using known intrinsics and
convert it to the same angular parameterization. The normalized camera ray is given by</p>
<table id="S2.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}(u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}(u-c_{x})/f_{x}\\
(v-c_{y})/f_{y}\\
1\end{bmatrix}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}(u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}(u-c_{x})/f_{x}\\
(v-c_{y})/f_{y}\\
1\end{bmatrix}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The azimuth and elevation angles are then computed as</p>
<table id="S2.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(u,v)=\arctan\!\left(\frac{r_{x}}{r_{z}}\right),\qquad\theta(u,v)=\arctan\!\left(\frac{r_{y}}{\sqrt{r_{x}^{2}+r_{z}^{2}}}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.760em;" width="2.760em"><mi>arctan</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.760em;" width="2.760em"><mi>arctan</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(u,v)=\arctan\!\left(\frac{r_{x}}{r_{z}}\right),\qquad\theta(u,v)=\arctan\!\left(\frac{r_{y}}{\sqrt{r_{x}^{2}+r_{z}^{2}}}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}(u,v)=[r_{x},r_{y},r_{z}]^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}(u,v)=[r_{x},r_{y},r_{z}]^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This representation naturally aligns sparse range observations with dense image pixels and avoids
projection ambiguities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We model depth as a latent function <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(\mathbf{a})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(\mathbf{a})</annotation></semantics></math> defined over the angular domain and adopt
Gaussian Process (GP) regression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rasmussen and Williams, 2006</a>)</cite> to infer dense depth values from
sparse observations.
We place a GP prior on <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(\mathbf{a})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(\mathbf{a})</annotation></semantics></math> with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel and assume
independent Gaussian measurement noise:</p>
<table id="S2.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,\kappa),\qquad z_{t}=Z(\mathbf{a}_{t})+n_{t},\ \ n_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{n}^{2})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,\kappa),\qquad z_{t}=Z(\mathbf{a}_{t})+n_{t},\ \ n_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{n}^{2}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Given sparse observations <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(\mathbf{a}_{t},z_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(\mathbf{a}_{t},z_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, the posterior predictive distribution
at a query angular location <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is Gaussian,</p>
<table id="S2.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\!\left(Z(\mathbf{a}_{\star})\mid\mathbf{A}_{T},\mathbf{z}_{T}\right)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star}),\,\sigma_{T}^{2}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.333em;" width="0.333em"><mi>p</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.798em;" width="0.798em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\!\left(Z(\mathbf{a}_{\star})\mid\mathbf{A}_{T},\mathbf{z}_{T}\right)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star}),\,\sigma_{T}^{2}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}_{T}=[\mathbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{a}_{T}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{T}=[\mathbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{a}_{T}]</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{T}=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{T}]^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{T}=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{T}]^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The posterior mean and variance are</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mu_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mu_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.E13"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sigma_{T}^{2}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sigma_{T}^{2}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{\star},\mathbf{a}_{\star})-\mathbf{k}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})^{\top}\left(\mathbf{K}_{T}+\sigma_{n}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{k}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐤</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐤</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{\star},\mathbf{a}_{\star})-\mathbf{k}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})^{\top}\left(\mathbf{K}_{T}+\sigma_{n}^{2}\mathbf{I}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{k}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\mathbf{K}_{T}]_{m,m^{\prime}}=\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{m},\mathbf{a}_{m^{\prime}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\mathbf{K}_{T}]_{m,m^{\prime}}=\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{m},\mathbf{a}_{m^{\prime}})</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{k}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})=\big[\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{\star}),\ldots,\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{T},\mathbf{a}_{\star})\big]^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐤</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{k}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})=\big[\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{\star}),\ldots,\kappa(\mathbf{a}_{T},\mathbf{a}_{\star})\big]^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The posterior mean serves as the reconstructed depth, while the predictive variance quantifies
uncertainty. Computing the full GP posterior scales as <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(T^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(T^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> in general. However,
depth is locally smooth in the angular domain, and depth at a given viewing direction is primarily
influenced by nearby range measurements, motivating a localized formulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We therefore adopt a per-query localized Gaussian Process formulation.
For each query angular location <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define a local neighborhood</p>
<table id="S2.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})=\left\{\mathbf{a}_{t}:\|\mathbf{a}_{t}-\mathbf{a}_{\star}\|_{2}\leq r\right\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})=\left\{\mathbf{a}_{t}:\|\mathbf{a}_{t}-\mathbf{a}_{\star}\|_{2}\leq r\right\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is a fixed angular radius.
Only range measurements within this circular neighborhood contribute to GP inference at
<math id="S2.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}_{T_{\star}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{T_{\star}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{T_{\star}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{T_{\star}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the measurements within
<math id="S2.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\star}\ll T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo>≪</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\star}\ll T</annotation></semantics></math> due to sparse sensing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">For each query, we use an RBF kernel</p>
<table id="S2.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{a}^{\prime})=\sigma_{f}^{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2\ell^{2}}\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{a}^{\prime})=\sigma_{f}^{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2\ell^{2}}\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> controls angular smoothness.
The signal variance <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{f}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{f}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is fixed based on prior knowledge of the sensing range, while the
length scale <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is selected via marginal likelihood maximization.
For each image pixel <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math>, we query the local GP centered at <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain a dense
depth estimate and its associated uncertainty. This per-query localized formulation reduces
computational complexity to <math id="S2.SS2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(T_{\star}^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mo>⋆</mo><mn>3</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(T_{\star}^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> per query and is trivially parallelizable
across image locations. Fig. <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Sparse Range-Sensor Depth Estimation via Gaussian Processes ‣ 2 Method ‣ A Single Image and Multimodality Is All You Need for Novel View Synthesis" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the localized GP formulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The predictive variance <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{T_{\star}}^{2}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{T_{\star}}^{2}(\mathbf{a}_{\star})</annotation></semantics></math> provides a principled measure of
depth reliability.
During geometric rendering, depth estimates whose variance exceeds a fixed threshold are masked
out, preventing unreliable geometry from contributing to the conditioning frames used by the
diffusion model.
This uncertainty-aware depth reconstruction yields more stable geometric conditioning and improves
the robustness and consistency of downstream novel-view synthesis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark</span>. In this work, we consider the RBF kernel for GP-based modeling. While existing works aim to identify the most appropriate kernel function <math id="S2.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> to effectively capture the covariance between function evaluations; see e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, they could be readily utilized in our proposed approach but this exceeds the scope of the current work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Dataset</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our method using the View-of-Delft (VoD) dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Palffy et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, a multi-modal autonomous driving dataset containing synchronized automotive radar, camera, and LiDAR data collected in urban environments. For evaluation, we curate a subset of 26 diverse video segments
spanning a range of urban scene types and capture conditions, which we use to benchmark single-image
novel-view synthesis performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Single View to Video Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the camera metadata provided with each VoD sequence to define a target camera trajectory for
novel-view synthesis. Concretely, we take the first frame of each sequence as the input reference
image and use the recorded camera poses from this first frame through the final frame to specify
the target trajectory along which novel views are synthesized. For geometry estimation, our method
reconstructs depth from synchronized sparse range measurements using the proposed Gaussian
process–based depth reconstruction module. We evaluate two multimodal variants: one using sparse
automotive radar measurements, which correspond to approximately 0.02% of image pixels, and one
using sparse LiDAR measurements, which correspond to approximately 0.52% of image pixels. In
contrast, the image-only baseline follows the default GEN3C pipeline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and
infers depth from the RGB input using the monocular depth estimator MoGe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
In all cases, the estimated depth is back-projected to form a colored 3D point cloud, which is
rendered along the target camera trajectory to produce sparse novel views with disoccluded and
unobserved regions. A diffusion-based inpainting stage then completes missing content to generate
a temporally consistent video along the specified camera path.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>
Quantitative evaluation on the View-of-Delft dataset for single-image novel-view video generation
with GEN3C <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite> under three depth-conditioning variants:
(i) the default pipeline using the vision-only monocular depth estimator MoGe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>,
(ii) the same pipeline with monocular depth replaced by our multimodal sparse range-sensor depth
reconstruction module using synchronized radar measurements (approximately 0.02% pixel coverage),
and (iii) the same replacement using synchronized LiDAR measurements (approximately 0.52% pixel coverage).
Metrics are computed with respect to ground-truth target views (higher is better for PSNR/SSIM;
lower is better for LPIPS/FID/temporal LPIPS), and the results show consistent improvements across
all measures when using our reconstructed depth, emphasizing the role of reliable depth priors in
diffusion-based novel-view synthesis from a single image.
</figcaption>
<div id="S3.T1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:397.5pt;height:38.1pt;vertical-align:-17.1pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-58.1pt,5.6pt) scale(0.773671848144723,0.773671848144723) ;">

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For evaluation, we compare the generated videos against the corresponding ground-truth frames
captured along the same trajectory. We report pixel-aligned PSNR and SSIM, perceptual similarity
via LPIPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, distributional quality via FID <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heusel et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, and
temporal consistency via temporal LPIPS. Quantitative results are summarized in
Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Single View to Video Generation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ A Single Image and Multimodality Is All You Need for Novel View Synthesis" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Replacing monocular depth with our multimodal depth
reconstruction consistently improves performance across all metrics. Using sparse radar
measurements, PSNR increases from 12.36 to 14.26 (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>15.4%), SSIM increases from 0.4561 to
0.4860 (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>6.6%), LPIPS decreases from 0.5804 to 0.4441 (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>23.5% reduction), FID
decreases from 152.62 to 82.41 (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>46.0% reduction), and temporal LPIPS decreases from
0.1117 to 0.0790 (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>29.3% reduction). Using sparse LiDAR measurements yields further
improvements, achieving a PSNR of 14.69, SSIM of 0.4971, LPIPS of 0.4230, FID of 71.91, and
temporal LPIPS of 0.0563. These results indicate that improving the reliability of geometric priors, particularly through
even sparse range sensing—translates directly into higher-fidelity and more temporally consistent
diffusion-based novel-view synthesis from a single image. We further provide qualitative
comparisons in Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Single View to Video Generation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ A Single Image and Multimodality Is All You Need for Novel View Synthesis" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, which corroborate these trends by showing improved
geometric alignment and reduced view-dependent artifacts when using our depth reconstruction.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17909v1/Presentation1.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:494/724;" width="494" height="724" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>
Qualitative comparison on single-image novel-view synthesis on the View-of-Delft dataset.
From left to right, we show the input image, the novel view generated by GEN3C <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite> using its default
monocular depth estimator, MoGe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, the novel view generated by GEN3C when replacing monocular depth with our
sparse range-sensor depth reconstruction module, and the ground-truth target view.
For each generated view, we report LPIPS with respect to the ground truth (lower is better).
Across all examples, our depth reconstruction yields consistently lower LPIPS and improved geometric alignment, underscoring the importance of reliable geometry for diffusion-based rendering from single-view inputs.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Depth Estimation Accuracy</h3>

<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>
Depth estimation accuracy on the View-of-Delft dataset evaluated on the first frame of each of the
26 selected segments. Our multimodal depth reconstruction uses synchronized radar measurements that
cover approximately 0.02% of image pixels. Predicted depth is compared against LiDAR-derived depth
at pixels where LiDAR measurements are available. Lower is better for both metrics.
</figcaption>
<div id="S3.T2.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:238.5pt;height:29.4pt;vertical-align:-13.2pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-80.3pt,9.9pt) scale(0.597706170889489,0.597706170889489) ;">

<th id="S3.T2.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><math id="S3.T2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MAE}\,\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>MAE</mi><mo lspace="0.448em" stretchy="false">↓</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MAE}\,\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></th>

<td id="S3.T2.2.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">2.23</td></tr>

<td id="S3.T2.2.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S3.T2.2.1.4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.92</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To directly assess the quality of the reconstructed depth, we evaluate depth estimation accuracy
on the View-of-Delft dataset using LiDAR-derived depth as ground truth. We conduct this evaluation on the first image of each of the 26 selected scenarios.
Depth predictions are evaluated at image pixels where LiDAR measurements are available, ensuring a
fair and consistent comparison across methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our sparse radar–based depth reconstruction against two representative monocular depth
estimators: MoGe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Depth Anything V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
All methods produce a dense depth map aligned with the reference image, which is then compared to
the corresponding LiDAR depth values at valid pixels.
We report mean absolute error (MAE) in linear depth and root mean squared error in log depth
(RMSE<sub id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">log</span></sub>), with lower values indicating more accurate depth estimation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Quantitative results are summarized in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Depth Estimation Accuracy ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ A Single Image and Multimodality Is All You Need for Novel View Synthesis" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Our method achieves the lowest error across both metrics, improving MAE from 14.25 to 13.61
(<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>4.5% relative reduction over the best monocular baseline, MoGe) and improving
<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{RMSE}_{\log}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>RMSE</mi><mi>log</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{RMSE}_{\log}</annotation></semantics></math> from 0.94 to 0.92 (<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>2.1% relative reduction over the best monocular
baseline, Depth Anything V2). These results indicate that incorporating sparse radar measurements
yields more accurate and reliable depth estimates than vision-only monocular approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduced a multimodal framework for single-image novel-view synthesis as an efficient and reliable alternative to vision-only diffusion-based counterpart. In addition to the visual information from the single view, we proposed a depth map reconstruction approach by
modeling sparse radar measurements via a computationally efficient principled localized Gaussian Process framework producing dense depth maps with spatially varying uncertainty. The estimated depth integrates seamlessly with existing diffusion-based rendering pipelines, improving geometric consistency and alignment across viewpoints. Experiments on diverse scenes from a real-world multimodal autonomous-driving database demonstrated that our approach resulted in significant improvements in downstream video generation quality compared to image-only baselines; hence justifying the claim that <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">a single image and multimodality is all you need for efficient 3D scene perception.</span> In our future research agenda, we aim to explore the benefits of the proposed depth and uncertainty representation for broader multimodal 3D perception tasks, including mapping, planning, and sensor fusion.</p>
</div>
</section>

      methods listed below:</p>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
